newsitem.title: GERMANY: Most German food firms seen buying gene-soybeans.
newsitem.headline: Most German food firms seen buying gene-soybeans.

text.p: Most of Germany's 5,000 food manufacturing firms have no plans to boycott soy oil derived from genetically altered U.S. soybeans currently under fire from a environmentalist campaign, industry sources said.
This offset public statements by brand leaders they would go without the new products for the time being.

"The majority of food producers are not relinquishing the use of soy oil," said Christiane Toussaint, adviser to Bonn-based institute BLL, which supplies scientific and legal services across the food industry.
"There are no boycott calls from the food trade either."
Led by environmentalist group Greenpeace, opponents say the new beans are a risky experiment with nature and human health although they have been approved by U.S. and EU authorities.
The beans, developed by U.S. chemicals firm Monsanto, have been made resistant to a widely used weedkiller.

Germany needs around 170,000 tonnes a month of U.S. soybeans for animal feed and for soy oil used in foods such as margarine. U.S. supplies account for nearly half of Germany's bean import total and Germany also imports readymade soy meal and oil.
Greenpeace said the list of companies averse to soy oil use was growing by the day and included 45 well-known firms.
"We have a sizeable number of large and medium-sized companies on the list, which is significant," said Joerg Naumann, Greenpeace campaign leader in Hamburg.
But an analyst said the fragmented nature of the market meant the vast majority of companies would carry on as normal.
"Even market leader Nestle accounts for just four percent of total food sales," he said.

A spokesman for Nestle in Germany reaffirmed it would bow to pressure and bar oil from genetically modified soybeans in this regional market. He said the company, where annual soy use amounts to 2,000 tonnes in some 3,000 products, was responding to consumer opposition, while the Nestle world group differed.
"We operate in 150 countries and regional centres can make their own marketing decisions," he said.
"If consumers here start accepting genetically engineered food products, we will reassess the current situation."
Food giant Anglo-Dutch Unilever pursues a similar policy at its German subsidiary, a leading margarine producer.
Seed crushers' organisation VDO in Bonn said processors did not expect the reactions to result in a sharp drop in domestic orders for soy oil, which was cheaper than other oils.
Vegetable oil traders in Britain and the Netherlands, the centres of vegetable protein trades in Europe, said the gene row was not affecting flows of soybeans, meal and oil.
In Germany, BLL's Toussaint said the industry would work towards better acceptance of biotechology and to help create practicable and useful labelling solutions for consumers.
